source.title: ScaMo: Exploring the Scaling Law in Autoregressive Motion Generation Model
source.authors: Shun-Lin Lu; Jingbo Wang; Zeyu Lu; Ling-Hao Chen; Wenxun Dai; Jun-Ting Dong; Zhi-Yang Dou; Bo Dai; Ruimao Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; the text ends with the limitations section.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law experiments to autoregressive text-driven human-motion generation, a modality outside language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling fits for normalized motion-token loss, vocabulary and non-vocabulary parameters, and data tokens. It also reports a large-run prediction check. The tokenizer comparisons and HumanML3D benchmark table are not recorded as scaling-law rows: they do not test the versions’ stated loss or downstream-task relationships. The study does not test language-model loss curves, architectural shape effects, or transfer to downstream language tasks.
record.test_reason: The study fits scaling relations in a new setting: text-driven autoregressive motion-token generation. It fits loss against compute (44M–3B models, about 10^14.5–10^18 FLOPs), fits compute-optimal allocation by power laws, and checks one larger-run prediction. These results bear on V5, and in this non-language setting on V2 and V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that normalized test loss follows a logarithmic law in FLOPs, and that optimal vocabulary parameters, non-vocabulary parameters and data tokens follow power laws in FLOPs. They also report a power law between vocabulary and non-vocabulary parameters, and say a 3B run at 1e18 FLOPs matched the predicted loss. In the limitations they add that data are limited and no emergent abilities were observed.
record.recipe_differences: This is a motion-generation extension, not a replication of language-model scaling experiments. It uses normalized conditional motion-token loss, varies vocabulary and non-vocabulary parameters, and fits optimal allocation against compute using least-squares estimation.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal vocabulary parameters scale as a power of non-vocabulary parameters: Nv = 10^-5.604·Nnv^1.467, R² = 0.95.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In tokenized generative models, the loss-optimal vocabulary size grows as a superlinear power of model size.

record.problems: The text gives no uncertainty estimates or numeric prediction error for the large-run validation. The central scaling evidence is reported as fitted curves and equations for one motion-generation system; no alternative fitting choices are compared.
record.rows_left_out: Tokenizer comparisons in Section 5.2 and Table 5, and generation benchmark metrics in Supplementary Table 6, were not extracted because they do not directly test the versions’ specified scaling-loss, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream-predictability relationships.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss. No text LM is trained; the only loss is a normalized motion-token loss.
Extrapolation over multiple orders of magnitude, and any quantitative prediction error.
Language-model allocation, and the Kaplan versus Hoffmann comparison under the standard parameter count. Here parameters are split into vocabulary and non-vocabulary parts.
No fixed-parameter comparison of shape. Depth and width covary across the configurations in Table 1.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
No alternative fitting methods, parameter counts or schedules are compared.

missing.what: Normalized loss against model size at each vocabulary size: larger models are consistently lower across all codebook sizes, and gains taper at large vocabularies. This bears on loss falling with parameters in the motion modality.
Downstream FID, R-precision and matching score across model and codebook sizes, plus the authors' note that these metrics diverge from normalized loss.

record.verdict_notes: Linking R2–R5 to V2 and V3 extends those versions to a non-language system; V5 is the primary fit. No uncertainty is reported for any fit, and the large-run check gives no numbers. The 1e18 FLOPs prediction point lies at the edge of the fitted range, not well beyond it. The paper's derived exponent ratios (1.325, 1.315) contain arithmetic errors. Tokenizer comparisons (Table 5) are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The models generate motion tokens rather than language, and the study does not measure language-model held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
The reported prediction check is for normalized motion-token loss in this motion-generation system; it does not establish extrapolation for language models.
The compute-optimal allocation is measured for this motion-generation system, including vocabulary and non-vocabulary parameters, not for language-model parameter counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests motion generation only; it does not test image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
The study does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or establish downstream predictability.
It does not compare alternative fitting choices or setups to test whether exponents change, or report systematic bending away from its fitted curves.

rows.subject: ScaMo models (44M–3B; aggregate scaling fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit normalized test loss against compute for optimal parameter and data settings.

conditions.value: FLOPs; fitted curve shown over approximately 10^14.5–10^18

rows.note: The paper reports a logarithmic relationship between compute and normalized test loss, rather than reporting a power-law loss fit.
rows.check: Loss falls smoothly with compute over about 3.5 decades. The authors assumed and fitted a log-linear form on a normalized loss that can be negative, not a power law, and compared no power-law alternative. That is a different functional form, not an absent effect, so 'observed' overstates the match to V5 and 'challenges' overstates the contrary evidence.

rows.subject: ScaMo models (aggregate compute-optimal fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit optimal vocabulary parameter count against compute.

conditions.value: parameter combinations minimizing test loss at each compute budget

rows.measure: Optimal vocabulary parameters Nv versus compute C
rows.note: A fitted power law for the compute-optimal vocabulary parameter count.
rows.check: Selection-based fit on IsoFLOP minima, motion domain only. No uncertainty or R² is given for this fit.

rows.subject: ScaMo models (aggregate compute-optimal fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit optimal non-vocabulary parameter count against compute.

conditions.value: parameter combinations minimizing test loss at each compute budget

rows.measure: Optimal non-vocabulary parameters Nnv versus compute C
rows.note: A fitted power law for the compute-optimal non-vocabulary parameter count.
rows.check: Motion domain only; no uncertainty reported.

rows.subject: ScaMo models (aggregate compute-optimal fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit optimal data-token count against compute.

conditions.value: parameter combinations minimizing test loss at each compute budget

rows.measure: Optimal data tokens D versus compute C
rows.note: A fitted power law for the compute-optimal data-token count.
rows.check: Motion domain only. The text's derived ratios are arithmetically wrong: 'Nnv/D ∝ C^1.325' should be C^0.14 from 0.57−0.43, and 'Nv/Nnv ∝ C^1.315' should be C^0.18. Its qualitative conclusion (scale Nnv faster than data) still follows.

rows.subject: ScaMo-3B
rows.operation_detail: Train a large model using the fitted compute-allocation and loss predictions, then compare its test loss with the prediction.

conditions.value: predicted optimal model size, vocabulary size, and data requirements

rows.measure: Predicted versus observed normalized test loss
rows.value: The paper states that the observed test normalized loss aligns precisely with the predicted loss.
rows.note: The paper gives no numeric loss value or prediction error for this comparison.
rows.check: No numeric observed loss, predicted loss or residual is given. The check is one run at about 1e18 FLOPs, the top end of the fitted compute range shown in Fig. 3(b), so it is far less than an orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The text also miscites Fig. 7(a) for this result.

rows.subject: ScaMo models (aggregate relationship)
rows.operation_detail: Fit vocabulary parameters as a function of non-vocabulary parameters.
rows.measure: Vocabulary parameters Nv versus non-vocabulary parameters Nnv
rows.value: Nv = 10^-5.604 · Nnv^1.467; the text also gives γ ≈ 1.46 and R² = 0.95.
rows.note: This is an additional reported power-law relation, not a compute-optimal parameter-versus-token fit.
rows.check: The fit of vocabulary parameters against non-vocabulary parameters (R²=0.95) is neither a loss law nor a parameter-versus-token compute allocation. It fits no version as stated.

relationships.condition: Motion generation; single 3B, 2^16-vocabulary run at about 1e18 FLOPs, near the top of the fitted range
relationships.reason: Authors state the observed normalized loss aligns with the prediction (R5), but give no number for the error.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported that observed normalized loss aligned with the prediction for the 3B motion-generation run.

relationships.condition: Compute-optimal allocation in ScaMo motion generation, about 10^14.5–10^18 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Optimal Nv, Nnv and D each fit a power of compute: exponents 0.75, 0.57 and 0.43 (R2–R4). Model size grows faster than data, in the Kaplan direction.
relationships.display_finding: Optimal Nv, Nnv, and training tokens followed compute exponents of 0.75, 0.57, and 0.43, respectively.

relationships.condition: Compute-optimal allocation in autoregressive motion generation
relationships.reason: Allocation quantities follow power laws in compute in a non-text modality (R2–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Compute-optimal allocation quantities followed power laws in compute for autoregressive motion generation.

relationships.condition: Normalized test loss versus compute in motion generation
relationships.reason: Loss falls steadily with compute but is fitted as logarithmic in C on a normalized loss, not as a power law (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Normalized test loss decreased steadily with compute but was fitted as logarithmic in C.

relationships.condition: HumanML3D benchmark metrics across 44M–3B models and codebook sizes (text-based; no row)
relationships.reason: Per Table 6, FID and R@1 mostly improve with model size, but not monotonically (e.g. 2048 codebook: 1B FID 0.320 vs 3B 0.346). Authors say the metrics are at times 'inconsistent with the normalized loss'.
relationships.display_finding: FID and R@1 generally improved but were non-monotonic and sometimes inconsistent with normalized loss, with FID worsening from 0.320 at 1B to 0.346 at 3B for the 2048 codebook.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
